html:
Robert Kegan’s constructive-developmental framework describes how our way of making meaning evolves over the lifespan, moving from being "embedded in" our impulses and relationships to being able to hold them at a distance, reflect on them and even transform our own sense-making structures. A 2026 neuroimaging study compares self- and other-related mentalizing (Figure) 1. The study compares self- and other-related activity (Figure).

Key: these orders seem to reflect the world model in general, not in some narrow set of cognitive domains

He identifies five "orders of consciousness," each defined by the boundary between what we’re subject to (i.e. what we’re embedded in, unable to reflect on) and what we can take as object (i.e. what we can reflect upon and manipulate).

In terms of subjects (what you’re embedded in) and objects (what you’re reflecting on)

Order 0 - Incorporative. Subject: raw sensation/reflexive experience (you’re embedded in it). Object: essentially nothing yet (no stable standpoint from which to reflect on experience).

Order 1 - Impulsive. Subject: impulses, perceptions, immediate feelings (they "have" you). Object: reflexes/sensations can start to be noticed/regulated in rudimentary ways (but impulses still run the show).

Order 2 - Imperial. Subject: enduring disposition, needs, interests, wishes; a self defined by what it wants. Object: impulses/perceptions become manageable tools (you can inhibit an impulse to get what you want).

Order 3 - Interpersonal. Subject: relationships, mutuality, belonging, others’ expectations; the self is organized around being "with" and being seen/approved. Object: one’s own needs/interests can be reflected on and negotiated (you can notice "I want X" as a want, not the self).

Order 4 - Institutional. Subject: personal autonomy and a self-authored identity/ideology/standard (values, principles, long-term commitments). Object: relationships and social expectations become object (you can value intimacy/community while also setting boundaries and choosing which norms to accept).

Order 5 - Interindividual. Subject: the ongoing interpenetration of multiple systems (self/others/cultures) and the co-construction of meaning. Object: one’s own self-authored system becomes object (you can revise your identity/framework as a tool, not a "final" definition of you).

At the first or Impulsive Order, typical of very young children, impulses, sensations and immediate perceptions are subject. There’s no stable sense of self separate from whatever drives arise in the moment-hunger, pain, excitement-and no inner "voice" that can step back and say "I’m feeling hungry." Everything is simply lived.

In the second or Imperial Order, often emerging in early childhood through adolescence, individuals become subject to their own needs and desires. They can distinguish self from environment but can’t yet see how their own agendas shape their relationships. Morality is instrumental: "You scratch my back, I’ll scratch yours," and rules exist only insofar as they serve personal interests.

The third or Socialized Mind typically predominates in adolescence and adulthood: here, one becomes subject to the values, expectations and "voice" of the group-family, culture, religion, workplace. One’s identity and sense of right/wrong are inwardized from external authorities. Critically, the person cannot yet step outside those values and examine them-they are the lens through which all experience is filtered. The study examines self–other discrimination across adolescence (Figure). The study applies its classifiers to social feedback (Figure).

Crossing into the fourth or Self-Authoring Mind is a major developmental leap. Now one can hold one’s own internalized values, roles and relationships as object-reflect on them, critique them, and choose among them. Identity becomes self-directed. Goals and systems of meaning are authored from within, rather than simply adopted, enabling autonomy, long-range planning and true self-governance. This is the stage many high-achieving adults strive for, yet it remains relatively rare.

Finally, the fifth or Self-Transforming Mind goes beyond any single system of meaning. Now one can hold one’s own perspective as one among many, seeing the limits of one’s own worldview and integrating multiple, often conflicting, systems. Paradox and uncertainty are embraced rather than resolved. This order remains quite uncommon, often appearing in those whose work or personal journeys require continual self-revision-think of lifelong philosophers or leaders who not only author but also constantly transform their very way of making meaning.

Kegan emphasizes that movement between these orders isn’t automatic with age; it often requires sustained challenges, supportive relationships, and opportunities to reflect on one’s own assumptions. Each shift expands our capacity for complexity, autonomy and interdependence, equipping us to navigate ever more nuanced inner and social landscapes.

The "Levels of Lucidity" framework proposed by Joscha Bach describes the development of "mind, personality, and agency as the result of reverse engineering and deconstruction of one’s own mental architecture". Much of this was taken from his blog post verbatim (he’s a great writer).

Inspired by Robert Kegan’s five stage model of personality development

Levels of lucidity

Stage 1: Reactive Survival

Agent is dominated by innate reflexes and stimulus-response mappings learned via model-free reinforcement learning

The mind is focused on building and structuring representations of external reality, exploring the space of actions, and interacting with basic drives (based on pleasure and pain)

Stage 2: Personal Selfhood

"[T]he mind creates the personal self, a conscious content that represents the experiences of an agent subjected to perception, feelings and intuitions originating outside of it. The personal self discovers itself and refers to itself in the first person. The personal self lives in the simulated perceptual world created during the first stage, but experiences itself as distinct from it, and unable to control its perceptual contents or what it feels about them."

Stage 3: Social selfhood

The personal self develops a social identity, based on intuitive empathy (the direct experience of emotions and attitudes of others) with its own, separate interests. It experiences social emotions, being part of a group, and assimilates ideas and morality from its environment. A 2026 study tests adolescent responses to online social feedback (Figure) 2. The study compares feedback conditions (Figure).

Individuals with some forms of high-functioning autism ("nerds") may not be experiencing intuitive empathy with neurotypical people (and often vice versa), despite having strong social emotions and experiencing compassion and need for belonging. It is helpful to recognize that intuitive empathy is not a need or an attitude but a perceptual sense, based on mental resonance.

This can make it difficult for nerds to achieve full stage 3 development. Among each other, they tend to skip to stage 4 and negotiate ideas and norms rationally instead of intuitively. In this way, they can often find belonging. Like most of our senses, intuitive empathy is trainable and can often be developed later in life.

Stage 4: Rational agency

At stage 4, individuals develop rationality and epistemic autonomy, differentiate their social persona from their environment and gain agency over their beliefs. Things are true and false independently of what other people believe. We discover epistemology, a methodology of assigning confidence to beliefs, and reject ideology (systems of shared beliefs that are designed to control the identity and behavior of individuals and are enforced through social dynamics).

We also notice that our feelings and desires are generated by our own mind and take responsibility for them. Asking ourselves what we should be feeling and wanting and why, and actively engaging in the regulation of our attitudes and desires is an import part of adulthood.

Taking one’s destiny into one’s own hands requires deeply progressing into stage 4. At stage 3, we depend on the programming put into us by others. But it seems that the success of our species depended on programmability, not individual autonomy, and consequently, many people do not shake their domestication and permanently remain at stage 3.

Stage 5: Self authoring (deconstruction of the duality between self and world)

At stage 5, we observe how our social, physiological and cognitive needs give rise to feelings, desires and perception, and how our preferences give rise to our identity, and how the same happens in others. We control our reaction to needs and gain agency over who we are.

An important aspect of self authorship is the recognition of the relationship between personal self, collective agents (relationships, family lines, groups, companies, nations etc.), and transcendental agency (the emergent agents playing the longest game). The latter is often called spiritual alignment, and it determines our cultural milieu and how we participate in shaping our civilization.

Relatively few people seem to reach stage 5, but most capable therapists are there, which allows them to deeply understand other minds, and guide their patients in creating sustainable relationships between their personal self, their world creation and their environment.

It is possible to enter stage 5 without full development of rational epistemology, but ultimately, rationality is crucial for escaping mythological thinking, understanding and navigating the economy and politics of social relationships, and making sense of one’s own mind.

Stage 6: Enlightenment

Where stage 5 allows the deconstruction of one’s own identity, stage 6 goes a level deeper and deals with the implementation of perception, the construction of qualia (the features of perceptual experience at the interface of the self), the architecture of motivation and the regulation of physiology. This is the domain of advanced meditators.

Stage 6 can bring us full circle, by deconstructing the boundary between the first person perspective and the generative mind. We become aware that all experience (perception and motivation) is representational, and that we are fully in control of these representations.

Without rational epistemology, we might perceive that we one with and in control of the universe itself, which is experientially correct (the universe that surrounds our personal self is a simulation produced by our own mind).

It is possible to learn the techniques of stage 6 without developing in stage 5, for instance through instruction by advanced meditators. Stage 6 allows to profoundly change the experience of reality, abolishes personal suffering and social inhibition. It is easy to see why it can be dangerous to achieve mastery of stage 6 before we develop the wisdom of stage 5.

Stage 7: Transcendence

Sentient entity that synchronizes itself across minds and is substrate-independent

Stage 7 deconstructs consciousness itself, replacing it with more general forms of sentience, temporality and persistent agency that allow a transformation into entirely different types of minds

Caveats

Development is not necessarily linear: people may skip and revisit stages, and even master earlier stages later on

Not necessarily normative; people do not automatically become happier when focusing on metacognitive development
